text: The highest Jewish council: about seventy members, led by the high priest and including elders and teachers of the law, who ruled on matters of religion and law.
The head of the priests of the temple in Jerusalem. In Roman times he led the Council and was the highest leader of Jewish society.
Harassing, imprisoning, or killing people because of their faith. After Stephen's death the first great persecution struck the church in Jerusalem.
The place where Jews gathered every Sabbath to read Scripture and pray. In each new city, Paul first preached in the synagogue.
Meaning 'son of a human being', the name Jesus often used for himself. In Daniel it refers to the one who comes with the clouds of heaven.
The Spirit of God, who lives in believers, gives them strength, and guides them. In Acts he opens the way for the church.
A scene God shows someone in a dream or while awake, to make his will known.
In Korean, literally 'holy ones': people who belong to God. It is a name for those who believe in Jesus.
A name for people who are not Jewish. Paul was called to be the apostle who brought the gospel to the Gentiles.
A rite of washing with water or being immersed in it, showing that sins are washed away and the person has become a follower of Jesus.
A Greek word meaning 'anointed one', the same as the Hebrew 'Messiah'. It refers to the Savior God promised.
Meaning 'one who belongs to Christ'. The people of Antioch were the first to call Jesus' disciples by this name.
A person who receives God's word and passes it on to others. There were prophets in the Old Testament and in the early church.
Older leaders who care for and guide a community. Paul appointed elders in each city and entrusted the church to them.
Meaning 'one who is sent': the twelve disciples Jesus himself appointed, and Paul, called by the risen Lord.
Going without food for a time to focus on God, practiced with prayer before important decisions.
Placing hands on a person's head or body and praying, done when sending someone out for a task, healing, or blessing.
An official Rome sent to rule a province. Cyprus and Achaia were ruled by governors sent by the Senate, Judea by governors sent by the emperor.
A person who claimed mysterious power through spells or fortune-telling and held people under his sway. The Bible forbade such things.
A person who passes off words God did not give as the word of God.
The seventh day of the week (sunset Friday to sunset Saturday), a day for resting from work and worshiping God.
The commandments and rules God gave through Moses. In a broader sense, the first five books of the Old Testament.

terms: law of Moses and the Prophets
text: 'The Prophets' are the books of prophets such as Isaiah and Jeremiah. In the synagogue they were read after the Law.
The person who organized the gatherings and worship of a synagogue and decided who would read and speak.
God accepting sinners as if they had no sin. Paul taught that this comes not by works but by faith.
A Jewish gesture showing that a town had rejected the message, so the responsibility now lay with them.
Women of high rank from wealthy families. They had great influence in Greek cities.
Worshiping a god by offering animals or grain. The people of Lystra thought Paul and Barnabas were gods and tried to offer sacrifices to them.
A person in charge of sacrifices at a temple. The priest at Lystra served the temple of Zeus.
A custom of tearing one's clothes to show great grief or to react to words that insult God.
The realm where God rules as king. It is less a place than God's rule being carried out.
A rite of cutting off the foreskin of a baby boy, the covenant sign of God's people. Whether Gentile believers also had to be circumcised was a great debate.
Meaning 'good news': the news that Jesus Christ died and rose again to save people.
The love and gifts God freely gives to people who have done nothing to deserve them.
Astonishing acts showing that God is present. The word puts weight on what a miracle points to.
A city where Rome settled people such as retired soldiers and granted Roman law and privileges. The people of Philippi were very proud of being Roman citizens.
Purple cloth dyed with a costly dye taken from sea snails. Only the rich and powerful wore it, so those who sold it did well.
A Gentile who was not Jewish but believed in the God of Israel and joined in synagogue worship.
A spirit said to foretell the future. Through the slave girl it possessed, her owners made money telling fortunes.
A wooden frame that locked a prisoner's ankles so he could not escape.
The person who guarded a prison and was in charge of the prisoners. If a prisoner escaped, he himself was punished.
Images of gods made by human hands and worshiped. Athens was full of statues of gods and altars of every kind.
Greek philosophers who made peace of mind and pleasure free from pain the goal of life. They held that the gods take no interest in human affairs.
Greek philosophers who taught people to govern their emotions by reason and to accept their fate.
Meaning 'hill of Ares'. Athens' ancient council met there and took its name from it; it sometimes examined new teachings.
Not just feeling sorry for wrongs, but turning the heart and the direction of life toward God.
God justly weighing the life of every person on the last day.
A dead person coming back to life. The resurrection of Jesus is at the center of the Christian faith.
The supreme ruler of the Roman Empire. In Paul's day the emperors were Claudius and Nero.
Tents were made of leather or goat-hair cloth. Paul earned his own living making tents while he preached the gospel.
A lecture hall in Ephesus. Tyrannus was probably its owner or a teacher there; Paul taught in it every day for two years.
Spiritual beings who oppose God and torment people. They left at the name of Jesus.
Coins made of silver, each usually worth about a day's wage for a laborer. Fifty thousand of them was an enormous sum.
The goddess Artemis worshiped by the Greeks. Her temple in Ephesus was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
A building where a god is housed and worshiped.
The highest official of Ephesus, in charge of the city's records and its assembly. He answered to Rome for order in the city.
Looking down on a god or something holy and treating it with contempt.
Money given to God or collected to help neighbors in need. Paul carried the gifts of the Gentile churches to the poor believers in Jerusalem.
A seven-day Jewish festival following Passover, when people ate bread without yeast to remember the exodus from Egypt.
Sharing bread together; in the early church it meant sharing the Lord's Supper.
A rite of sharing bread and cup in memory of the last meal Jesus ate with his disciples the night before he died. It is also called Communion.
A large room on the upper floor of a house. The early church gathered in rooms like this to worship.
A Jewish harvest festival on the fiftieth day after Passover. Many pilgrims gathered in Jerusalem on that day.
Suffering and hardship that are hard to bear.
Being tied up with ropes or chains; here, a sign that Paul would be arrested and imprisoned.
A person whose work is spreading the gospel. Philip was one of the seven helpers of the Jerusalem church.
A rite under the law for making the body clean. Paul took part in it with four men who were completing a Nazirite vow.
A Roman officer in command of about a thousand soldiers. He led the garrison of the Antonia Fortress in Jerusalem.
Quarters where soldiers stay. In Jerusalem this means the Antonia Fortress right beside the temple.
A Roman officer in command of about a hundred soldiers, the professional soldiers who formed the backbone of the army.
Roman citizens had the privilege of not being flogged without trial and of appealing to the emperor. Paul was a citizen from birth.
A Jewish group centered on priestly families and the wealthy. They accepted only the five books of Moses and did not believe in resurrection or angels.
A Jewish group devoted to keeping the law and the traditions of the elders in every detail. They believed in the resurrection, and Paul was a Pharisee.
Originally meaning 'party' or 'faction'. The accusers used it to brand the followers of Jesus as a false faction.
Governing one's own desires and feelings so as not to go too far.
A title for the Roman emperor, from the name Julius Caesar. The Caesar of Paul's day was Nero.
Refusing to accept a lower court's verdict and asking a higher authority to judge the case again. Roman citizens could appeal to the emperor.
A Roman auxiliary unit named after the emperor (Augustus).
A day each autumn (the tenth day of the seventh Jewish month) of fasting and praying for the people's sins to be cleansed. After it, sailing the Mediterranean became dangerous.
A violent northeast wind that blew over the Mediterranean in winter, sweeping down from the mountains of Crete onto the sea.
A small boat carried by a large ship, used to carry people in danger or to go back and forth to shore.
Castor and Pollux, the twin sons of Zeus. Sailors honored them as gods who protected voyages and put their emblem on the bow.
The elite troops who guarded the Roman emperor. The soldiers guarding the imprisoned Paul took turns, and so heard the gospel.
Records of a family line from ancestors to descendants. False teachers in Ephesus stirred up empty arguments over them.
A wreath worn by the winner of a contest or by a king. Paul compared it to the reward for those who keep the faith to the end.
Writing material made by stretching and drying thin sheets of sheep or goat skin. These were probably precious scrolls of Scripture.
An offering of wine poured over a sacrifice (a drink offering). Paul compared his life to it, being poured out as an offering.
A raised platform built to offer sacrifices or worship a god.
